articles.title: The Letter That Wanted to Be a Visit
articles.dek: Samuel Morse built a wire to outrun grief. Centuries earlier, an old apostle set down his pen with a quieter idea about how love travels.
articles.quote: Ink can carry the truth across a great distance, but only presence can carry love the last few steps.
articles.body:
In February 1825, a young painter named Samuel Morse was in Washington working on the most important commission of his life, a full-length portrait of the Marquis de Lafayette for the city of New York. He was proud and hopeful, and he wrote home to his wife, Lucretia, in New Haven about how well the sittings were going. Then a letter arrived from his father. Lucretia had fallen suddenly ill after the birth of their third child, and she had died. The letter had taken days to reach him by horse and coach. Morse left at once, but by the time he reached Connecticut his wife was already buried.

Historians who tell Morse's story often point to that week as the wound behind what came next. The painter turned his restless mind toward a question that would not leave him: could a message travel faster than a horse? Nearly twenty years later, on May 24, 1844, he sat in the Supreme Court chamber of the Capitol and tapped out a line of dots and dashes that raced along a wire to Baltimore. The words, chosen by a young friend named Annie Ellsworth, came from the Bible: "What hath God wrought" (Numbers 23:23, KJV). A grieving man had helped shrink the distance between people who love each other, and every video call a Filipino family makes across oceans today stands somewhere downstream of that afternoon.

Yet Morse knew better than anyone that a faster message would not have given him what he truly wanted that winter. He wanted to be in the room with Lucretia. Long before telegraphs, an old man in the first century felt the same ache, and he said so at the end of one of the shortest books in the Bible.

Second John is barely thirteen verses long, small enough to fit on a single sheet of papyrus. Its writer calls himself simply "the elder," and the church has long understood him to be the apostle John, by then an aged pastor overseeing congregations around Ephesus. He addresses his letter "to the lady chosen by God and to her children, whom I love in the truth" (2 John 1:1). Many scholars read this "lady" as a warm, coded name for a local church, with "her children" being its members, especially since the letter closes with greetings from "the children of your sister, who is chosen by God" (2 John 1:13), which sounds like one congregation greeting another. Whether she was a church or a real hostess, the elder writes to her like a grandfather writing to family.

The letter moves quickly. John begins with delight: "It has given me great joy to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as the Father commanded us" (2 John 1:4). He reminds them of the oldest instruction they have: "I ask that we love one another. And this is love: that we walk in obedience to his commands" (2 John 1:5–6). Then his tone sharpens with real concern. Traveling teachers were going from house to house, and some of them were spreading a teaching that sounded spiritual and sophisticated. "Many deceivers, who do not acknowledge Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh, have gone out into the world" (2 John 1:7). These teachers held that God could never truly take on a human body, so Jesus only seemed to be flesh and blood. John tells the church plainly not to give such teachers a platform in their homes (2 John 1:10). In a world without hotels, where the church met in living rooms, opening your door to a traveling teacher amounted to endorsing him.

And then, just as the letter seems to be gathering strength, the old apostle puts down his pen.

"I have much to write to you, but I do not want to use paper and ink. Instead, I hope to visit you and talk with you face to face, so that our joy may be complete." (2 John 1:12)

At first this sounds like an ordinary sign-off, the kind of line we write at the bottom of a card. The words underneath are richer than that. "Paper" translates the Greek chartēs, a sheet of papyrus, and "ink" is melan, literally "black," the soot-and-gum mixture scribes used. The phrase NIV renders "face to face" is, in Greek, stoma pros stoma, "mouth to mouth." It is the same picture the Old Testament uses for the closeness God shared with Moses. "With him I speak face to face," the Lord says, "clearly and not in riddles" (Numbers 12:8), and the Hebrew there is also "mouth to mouth." John is reaching for the most intimate kind of speaking the Scriptures know.

The deeper surprise comes when you lay verse 12 beside verse 7. The very heresy John is warning against is the claim that God would never come in the flesh. Everything in John's life rose up against that idea. This is the man who wrote that "the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us" (John 1:14), and who opened his first letter with what he had "seen with our eyes," what "we have looked at and our hands have touched" (1 John 1:1). One way to read the close of this little letter, then, is as John practicing what he believes. A God who came in a body to save us is a God whose people will want to show up in body for one another. The doctrine of the Incarnation, the truth that God became human, quietly shapes the way the elder loves his church. He will not settle for sending ideas when he can bring himself.

Look also at the goal he names: "so that our joy may be complete." The word is peplērōmenē, filled to the brim. John had heard Jesus use the same language at the Last Supper: "I have told you this so that my joy may be in you and that your joy may be complete" (John 15:11). In John's mind, joy reaches its fullness when people who share the truth finally share a room. He even repeats the thought almost word for word in his next letter: "I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face" (3 John 1:14). This was clearly the habit of an old man's heart.

For many Filipino families, this lands close to home. We have become experts at loving across distance. We send balikbayan boxes packed to the seams, we stay up past midnight for a call from Riyadh or Toronto, and we know the particular sound of a lola laughing through a frozen screen. These are real gifts, and Samuel Morse would be amazed by them. John never scorned his ink, either; he used it to write the letter we are reading. Ink can carry the truth across a great distance, but only presence can carry love the last few steps. The letter was the bridge, and the visit was always the destination.

That gives us a gentle question for this week. Somewhere near you is a person whom you have been loving mostly by message: a friend whose chats you always react to with a heart, a parent you call dutifully, a fellow believer you pray for from afar. If a visit is possible, consider making one before Sunday, and when you arrive, let it be unhurried. Bring merienda, sit longer than is convenient, and say the encouraging thing out loud that you would normally type. If distance truly makes that impossible, turn the camera on and look at their face while you speak, because John's hope was that the people he loved would see his face and hear his voice.

The elder never knew about telegraphs or fiber-optic cables, but he knew something that outlasts all of them. God did not love the world from a safe distance; he came near enough to be touched. Every time you choose to show up in person for someone, you are telling them a small version of that same good news, and you may find, as John hoped, that your own joy is filled to the brim along with theirs.

articles.title: The Voice That Calls You Home
articles.dek: When Israel wandered after other lovers, God answered with a courtship. In Hosea 2, the valley named for trouble becomes a door of hope.
articles.quote: God meets our wandering by following us into the wilderness and speaking to our hearts until we recognize his voice again.
articles.body:
In the middle of the Antarctic winter, on sea ice where the temperature can drop below minus forty degrees, thousands of male emperor penguins stand huddled together, each balancing a single egg on his feet. They have eaten nothing for weeks. Their mates left soon after laying, walking many kilometres across the ice to the open ocean to feed, and they will be away for roughly two months. When the females finally come back, fat and glossy from the sea, they face what looks like an impossible problem. The colony has no nests and no landmarks, only a shifting crowd of birds that look almost exactly alike.

How they solve it is one of the loveliest discoveries in animal behavior. The French researchers Pierre Jouventin and Thierry Aubin found that emperor penguins sing with two voices at once. Their vocal organ, the syrinx, has two sides, and each side can produce its own tone at the same moment, so the two frequencies beat against each other and form a pattern unique to that bird, a kind of acoustic fingerprint. A returning female walks into the roar of the colony, calls, and listens. Somewhere in that crowd one particular bird hears the voice he has been waiting for and answers, and the two find each other by sound alone. Their chick will learn the same skill, picking out a parent's call among thousands. In a place where everything looks the same, love finds its way home by voice.

Older Filipinos remember a gentler, warmer version of this. A young man would stand beneath a window at night with a guitar and a few brave friends and sing the harana, hoping his voice would reach the one inside. Courtship by voice asks for patience, and it assumes the heart can be won by being spoken to. That Antarctic colony and that old serenade both help me hear one of the most tender passages in the Old Testament, where God decides to win back his people by speaking to their hearts.

Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century before Christ, during the long and prosperous reign of Jeroboam II. Harvests were good and markets were busy, but the people had drifted into the worship of Baal, the Canaanite storm god who was believed to send rain and make the fields fruitful. God gave Hosea a painful assignment that would turn his own home into a sermon: "Go, marry a promiscuous woman and have children with her, for like an adulterous wife this land is guilty of unfaithfulness to the LORD" (Hosea 1:2). Hosea married Gomer, and their children carried names that sounded like verdicts. A daughter was called Lo-Ruhamah, which means "not loved" (Hosea 1:6), and a son was called Lo-Ammi, "not my people" (Hosea 1:9).

In chapter 2, the marriage and the nation blur together. The wife leaves, saying, "I will go after my lovers, who give me my food and my water, my wool and my linen, my olive oil and my drink" (Hosea 2:5). The tragedy is that every one of those gifts had come from the husband she abandoned: "She has not acknowledged that I was the one who gave her the grain, the new wine and oil" (Hosea 2:8). Israel had been thanking Baal for the rain God sent. So God says, "Therefore I will block her path with thornbushes" (Hosea 2:6), and a second "therefore" in verse 9 announces that he will take back the grain and wool. Any reader expects a third "therefore" to bring the final sentence of judgment. Instead, it brings this:

"Therefore I am now going to allure her; I will lead her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her. There I will give her back her vineyards, and will make the Valley of Achor a door of hope. There she will respond as in the days of her youth, as in the day she came up out of Egypt." (Hosea 2:14–15)

The same word that introduced the consequences now introduces a courtship. One way to read this is that the thornbushes were never the point. God blocked the roads to her other lovers so that she would be alone long enough to hear him. The Hebrew behind "speak tenderly" is literally dibber al-lev, "to speak to the heart." It is the phrase used when Joseph reassured the brothers who had sold him (Genesis 50:21), when Ruth thanked Boaz for having "spoken kindly" to her (Ruth 2:13), and when Isaiah was told to "speak tenderly to Jerusalem" after her long exile (Isaiah 40:2). It is the language of a wooer under a window, and God uses it of himself.

The place he chooses matters too. The wilderness was where the romance first began. Jeremiah would later hear God say, "I remember the devotion of your youth, how as a bride you loved me and followed me through the wilderness" (Jeremiah 2:2). God is taking his people back to the place where they had nothing but manna and his voice, and where they were happiest. Then he names a second place, the Valley of Achor. Achor means "trouble," and it was the valley where Achan's sin brought disaster on Israel as they entered the land (Joshua 7:24–26). It was a name that recalled shame. God promises to turn that very valley into a petach tikvah, a doorway of hope. He does not lead his people around their place of trouble; he puts a door in it.

What follows is a proposal. "You will call me 'my husband'; you will no longer call me 'my master'" (Hosea 2:16). The word for master is baal, and God wants even that word gone from her mouth (Hosea 2:17). He desires closeness, a relationship of mutual knowing in place of ownership. Then comes the vow: "I will betroth you to me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in love and compassion. I will betroth you in faithfulness, and you will acknowledge the LORD" (Hosea 2:19–20). In Israel the groom paid the bride-price, and here God pays it himself, with his own character. The word "compassion" in that vow comes from the same root as ruhamah. The girl once named "not loved" is about to receive her new name: "I will show my love to the one I called 'Not my loved one.' I will say to those called 'Not my people,' 'You are my people'; and they will say, 'You are my God'" (Hosea 2:23). Centuries later, Paul and Peter would quote those words to welcome Gentiles into God's family (Romans 9:25; 1 Peter 2:10).

Chapter 3 shows Hosea living out the sermon. God tells him, "Go, show your love to your wife again" (Hosea 3:1), and Hosea buys Gomer back for fifteen shekels of silver and some barley (Hosea 3:2), paying for a woman who was already his. Grace often looks like this, and it can make us uncomfortable, because it is so much more generous than we would be.

Perhaps you are in a dry season right now. The things you leaned on for security have stopped working, and the paths you used to take feel blocked by thorns. Hosea suggests a gentle way to read that season. The wilderness may be the very place where God has stopped the noise long enough to speak to your heart. The question is whether we have been crediting our blessings to other sources, such as our salary, our cleverness, or our connections, when the grain and the oil came from him all along. God meets our wandering by following us into the wilderness and speaking to our hearts until we recognize his voice again.

This passage also carries quiet wisdom for our human relationships. When someone we love has drifted or wounded us, our instinct is to argue, accuse, or wait for them to grovel. God models something better: he speaks to the heart, he returns to the memories of first love, and he offers a new name in place of the old label. You might take ten unhurried minutes today, read Hosea 2:14–23 aloud, and hear your own name where Israel's stands. Then think of one person who has grown distant and send them a few words that speak to their heart. Like a penguin calling across the ice, keep calling, because the One who loves you has never stopped calling you.

articles.title: The Week the Charts Turned Red
articles.dek: Psalm 135 warns that we slowly take on the likeness of whatever we trust. A struggling carmaker learned the same thing around a boardroom table, and its story points to the cure.
articles.quote: We slowly become like whatever we trust, which is the best reason to keep our faces turned toward the God who is alive.
articles.illustration: Alan Mulally's red slide at Ford
articles.body:
In the autumn of 2006, Alan Mulally walked into Ford Motor Company as its new chief executive. He was an engineer from Boeing who knew far more about airplanes than automobiles, and he had arrived at a company in deep trouble. Ford would lose more than twelve billion dollars that year, the worst loss in its long history. Every Thursday morning Mulally gathered his senior leaders around one table for what he called the Business Plan Review, and he asked each of them to mark their projects with a simple color: green for on track, yellow for a concern, red for a real problem.

For weeks, every chart came in green. Finally Mulally set down his papers and asked, as gently as he could, how a company losing billions of dollars could have nothing at all going wrong. The room went silent. Years in a culture where bad news could end a career had taught these capable men and women to protect the picture instead of telling the truth. They had built a reporting system to help them see, and over time it had trained them to look away.

Then one Thursday, Mark Fields, who ran Ford's operations in the Americas, put up a red slide. A new vehicle, the Edge, had a mechanical problem, and he had stopped its launch. Some of the executives in the room later admitted they expected Fields to be gone by the following week. Mulally began to clap instead. "Mark, that is great visibility," he said, and then he asked the table who could help. By the next Thursday the charts arrived in every color of the rainbow. Within three years Ford was profitable again, and it was the only one of Detroit's three big automakers to come through the 2008 financial crisis without a government bailout. Many who sat at that table trace the turnaround to a single honest slide.

I have been thinking about that boardroom while reading Psalm 135, because the psalm describes something very similar happening inside the human heart. Psalm 135 is a temple song, one of the "Hallelujah" psalms that open and close with the Hebrew words hallelu Yah, "Praise the LORD." Many scholars believe it was sung by worshipers and priests together in the temple courts, and it gathers lines from older Scripture, especially Psalm 115 and Deuteronomy 32, into one great anthem. The first half rehearses what God has done. He makes the clouds rise and sends lightning with the rain (Psalm 135:7). He struck down the firstborn of Egypt and brought his people out (Psalm 135:8–9). He gave them a land as an inheritance (Psalm 135:12).

Then, at verse 15, the singers turn and look across the border at the gods of the surrounding nations. In the ancient world an idol was a costly and beautiful thing. Isaiah and Jeremiah describe how one was made: a craftsman cut a tree, carved it, and a goldsmith overlaid it with gold and fastened it with nails so it would not totter (Isaiah 40:19–20; Jeremiah 10:3–4). In Mesopotamia, priests even performed a ceremony called the "washing of the mouth" and "opening of the mouth," meant to bring the statue to life so the god could dwell in it. The psalmist looks at all that skill and gold and ritual and describes what is really standing there: "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by human hands. They have mouths, but cannot speak, eyes, but cannot see. They have ears, but cannot hear, nor is there breath in their mouths" (Psalm 135:15–17).

The word for "breath" in verse 17 is the Hebrew ruach, which can mean breath, wind, or spirit. The same psalm has already used it once. In verse 7, the LORD "brings out the wind from his storehouses," and the word there is ruach as well. One way to read the psalm is to hear the singers setting the two pictures side by side on purpose: the living God keeps whole storehouses of wind, while the gods of gold cannot manage a single breath of their own. Then comes the line that gives the whole passage its weight.

"Those who make them will be like them, and so will all who trust in them." (Psalm 135:18, NIV)

This is a sobering promise, and also a deeply hopeful one. The psalm teaches that worship shapes the worshiper. The craftsman shaped gold into something that could not hear, and slowly, without his noticing, the gold shaped him back. A person who trusts what cannot see begins to lose sight, and a person who leans on what cannot speak gradually loses the words that matter. Jesus spoke of the same condition when he quoted Isaiah about people who are "ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding" (Mark 4:12). Like those green charts at Ford, our idols promise to help us see clearly and end up teaching us to look away.

Few of us keep a statue on a shelf, yet most of us know what it is to lean our full weight on something that cannot hold it. It might be a reputation we polish carefully, a bank balance we check more often than we pray, or the approval of people whose opinion has quietly become the voice we obey. These things are rarely evil in themselves. The danger is that when we trust them for what only God can give, they make us a little more like them: guarded, unable to admit a red slide, and short of breath.

What moves me most is how the psalm responds to its own warning. Right after verse 18, there is no lecture and no list of rules. The singers simply turn and begin to call people into praise, in ever-widening circles: "All you Israelites, praise the LORD; house of Aaron, praise the LORD; house of Levi, praise the LORD; you who fear him, praise the LORD" (Psalm 135:19–20). The house of Aaron were the priests and the house of Levi were the temple servants, and many scholars understand "you who fear him" to include people from other nations who had come to trust Israel's God. The circle keeps opening until there is room for anyone. The psalm's answer to becoming like a dead idol is to turn and face the living God, because the same law works in both directions. Paul describes it beautifully: "And we all, who with unveiled faces contemplate the Lord's glory, are being transformed into his image with ever-increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:18).

That transformation often begins with the kind of honesty that took courage in Ford's boardroom. Before you sleep tonight, you might ask the Lord, quietly and without fear, what you have been trusting to keep you safe, and then tell him plainly about one area of your life that is really in the red. You do not need to dress it up in green for him. The God of Psalm 135 has eyes that see, ears that hear, and breath to give, and Scripture invites us to "approach God's throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need" (Hebrews 4:16). He meets an honest heart with welcome, much as Mulally met Mark Fields, and then he gets to work helping.

We slowly become like whatever we trust, which is the best reason to keep our faces turned toward the God who is alive. Every honest prayer and every simple word of praise is a small turning of the face toward him, and over the years those small turnings add up to a changed life. So let the last line of the psalm be your own today, spoken softly wherever you are: "Praise be to the LORD from Zion, to him who dwells in Jerusalem. Praise the LORD" (Psalm 135:21).

articles.title: The Answer Standing at the Podium
articles.dek: A father in Proverbs expects his child's life to answer everyone who mocks him. The gospel shows how that answer was finally given, and how your ordinary days can join it.
articles.quote: Your faithful, ordinary life, carried by his grace, becomes the Father's glad answer to a doubting world.
articles.body:
On May 6, 2014, Kevin Durant stood at a podium in Oklahoma City to accept the National Basketball Association's Most Valuable Player award, and within a few minutes he was crying too hard to keep his voice steady. He thanked his teammates one by one, then his coaches, and then he turned toward the front row, where his mother, Wanda, was sitting. He told the room what she had done when he and his older brother, Tony, were boys: how she had raised them alone, kept them off the street, and put clothes on their backs and food on the table. "When you didn't eat, you made sure we ate," he said. "You went to sleep hungry. You sacrificed for us." Then he gave her the line that has been replayed millions of times since: "You the real MVP."

The cameras found Wanda wiping her eyes, and people who had never watched a basketball game wept along with her. Part of what moved them was simple gratitude, but something deeper was happening in that room. A single mother who had spent years doing the hard, unseen work of raising two boys with very little was hearing her son tell the whole world that it had been worth it. Whatever anyone had once said about her circumstances or her chances, the answer was standing at the podium in a tailored suit, saying her name.

An old proverb describes that moment almost exactly. It sits in the middle of Proverbs 27, among sayings about friends, neighbors, and leaky roofs, and it is easy to read past. Chapters 25 to 29 form a collection of Solomon's proverbs that, according to Proverbs 25:1, were "compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah," roughly two centuries after Solomon's reign. Most of these sayings are short, observant, and a little wry. Verse 14 warns that a neighbor who "loudly blesses" you early in the morning will be heard as cursing you, and verse 15 compares a quarrelsome home to "the dripping of a leaky roof in a rainstorm," a picture any Filipino who has set out a batya under the ceiling during habagat season understands at once. Yet in verse 11 the tone softens, and the tender voice of the book's opening chapters returns: a father speaking to his child.

"Be wise, my son, and bring joy to my heart; then I can answer anyone who treats me with contempt." (Proverbs 27:11)

The first half of the verse is familiar. Proverbs 10:1 says nearly the same thing: "A wise son brings joy to his father." Parents everywhere know that their happiness rises and falls with their children's choices, and Filipino parents, who so often pour their whole lives into their children's future, know it more deeply than most. The second half of the verse carries the surprise. This father has critics, people who look at him with contempt, and he expects his child's life to become his reply.

The Hebrew wording sharpens the picture. Literally, the father says, "that I may return a word to the one who taunts me." The word for the taunter, chorephi, comes from the verb charaph, which means to reproach, mock, or defy. It is the same verb used of Goliath when he strode into the Valley of Elah and shouted, "This day I defy the armies of Israel!" (1 Samuel 17:10). It appears again in Psalm 119:42, where the psalmist prays, "then I can answer anyone who taunts me, for I trust in your word." The two verses read like cousins. In both places, the answer to mockery is a life that holds steady, and in both, that steadiness is rooted in trust.

One way to read the proverb, then, is that a father's good name is bound up with what his children become. In the ancient Near East a household's honor was shared by everyone in it. A son's foolishness shamed the whole family, and his wisdom vindicated it. When the neighbors sneered that the father was too soft or too strict, he did not need to win the argument at the city gate. He could simply point to his son and let the young man's character speak for him.

Scripture widens that frame until it reaches God himself, because God has been taunted too. From the garden onward, the accusation has been that he cannot be trusted, that his ways are not good, and that no one could actually live wisely in his world and be glad of it. Israel's long history often seemed to prove the mockers right, and if we are honest, our own lives have given the Father's critics plenty to say. We are the children whose stumbling has made the family look foolish.

Then Jesus came. As he rose from the waters of the Jordan, a voice from heaven said, "This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). Here at last was the wise Son of Proverbs 27:11, whose every word and step brought joy to his Father's heart. When Satan taunted him in the wilderness, he answered with Scripture. When soldiers mocked him at the cross, he prayed, "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34). His obedience all the way to death, and his resurrection on the third day, became the Father's final word to every voice that had ever called God unfaithful.

This is where the proverb turns from a demand into good news. If you belong to Christ, the charges against you have already been answered by Someone else. Paul asks, "Who will bring any charge against those whom God has chosen? It is God who justifies" (Romans 8:33). You are already a beloved child, and your place in the family rests on what the Son has done. That settled love is what frees you to do what verse 11 invites: to live in a way that brings your Father joy, moved by gratitude instead of fear.

On an ordinary Wednesday, that kind of life will usually look small. Peter wrote to scattered believers who were being slandered, and his counsel was practical: "Live such good lives among the pagans that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us" (1 Peter 2:12). A coworker who thinks faith is for weak people may never read a book of apologetics (a reasoned defense of Christian belief), but they will watch how you handle a tight deadline, a rude client, or a mistake you could easily hide. Relatives who privately think your faith is a phase will see whether you are gentler at the Noche Buena table this year. Each of these moments is a small word returned to the Father's critics.

Before today ends, you might choose one place in your life that your Father would love to point to, perhaps a conversation you have been avoiding, a habit you keep excusing, or a person you quietly wrote off, and bring wisdom and kindness to it. When you fail, as all of us will, go back to the Son who has already answered for you. Receive his forgiveness, rest in his welcome, and begin again in the morning with the same grace that carried you yesterday.

After that night in Oklahoma City, Wanda Durant never needed to defend her parenting to anyone again, because her son's grateful words had said everything. You have a Father who delights in you more than any parent has ever delighted in a child; Zephaniah 3:17 promises that he "will take great delight in you" and "rejoice over you with singing." Your faithful, ordinary life, carried by his grace, becomes the Father's glad answer to a doubting world. Live today as a child who is already loved, and let him point to you with joy.
